title: CELPIP Reading Practice Test 14
instructions: Read each passage carefully and answer the questions. You may scroll back within each part.

emails.subject: Referral received 6 May — no appointment offered
emails.body:
Dear Meadowbank Physiotherapy,

My doctor sent a referral for shoulder rehabilitation on 6 May. It is now 18 June and I have had no appointment and no contact.

I telephoned twice. On 22 May I was told the wait was "about four weeks". On 9 June I was told the wait was "about four weeks". Both cannot be right, and if the second was accurate then the first was not.

I want to be fair about one thing: nobody has been rude to me, and I understand a clinic cannot invent capacity it does not have. If the answer is that the wait is four months, I would rather be told four months. What I cannot plan around is being told four weeks twice, six weeks apart.

My employer has asked when I will be fit for full duties and I have nothing to tell them. That is the practical cost of this, and it is not the clinic's fault that I have a job — but it is why an accurate number matters more than a comforting one.

Sincerely,
Gulnara Tashkentova

emails.subject: RE: Referral received 6 May — no appointment offered
emails.body:
Dear Ms Tashkentova,

You were given the same figure twice and it was wrong both times. I am not going to soften that.

Your referral is on our list and was never lost. The realistic wait for routine shoulder rehabilitation is currently fourteen to sixteen weeks, which from 6 May means mid-August. That is the number you should plan around and the number you should give your employer.

Why you were told four weeks: our reception staff read the wait from a figure that covers all referral types, and urgent post-surgical cases move through in three to five weeks. Averaged together the number looks like four. It is accurate for the list as a whole and useless for any individual on it, and telling you it was the fastest way to give you a comforting answer that was not true.

From next week reception quotes the wait for your referral category, and where we do not know, they will say so rather than reach for the average.

Two things you can act on now. There is a cancellation list you were never offered — say the word and I will add you today; short-notice slots come up most weeks. And your referral is marked routine. If your shoulder has worsened since 6 May, ask your doctor to review the priority, because that is a clinical decision we cannot make from here and it does change the queue.

Regards,
Daniel Oyelaran
Practice Manager

passages.title: Why Health Advice Keeps Changing
passages.content:
Few things erode public trust in health guidance more reliably than watching it reverse. A food is protective, then neutral, then suspect. A screening test is recommended for everyone, then for a narrower group. To a reasonable observer this looks like incompetence. It is usually something less dramatic and more structural.

Most nutritional and lifestyle guidance begins in observational research, which measures what people already do and what happens to them. That design can establish association and cannot establish cause, because the people who do one thing differ systematically from those who do not in ways no adjustment fully removes. Someone who eats more vegetables also tends to exercise more, smoke less and have more money. When a trial later isolates the single variable, the effect frequently shrinks or disappears — and the guidance changes not because the earlier work was fraudulent but because it was answering a weaker question.

Screening reversals follow a different logic and are more counter-intuitive. Detecting disease earlier sounds unambiguously good, and for some conditions it is. But screening also finds abnormalities that would never have caused harm, and every one of those leads to investigation and sometimes treatment with real risks. When a recommendation narrows, it is usually because the harms of over-diagnosis in a low-risk group were found to outweigh the benefit — a genuine finding that is almost impossible to communicate without sounding like rationing.

Reporting compounds all of this. A study reporting that a behaviour raises a risk by fifty per cent is describing relative risk. If the underlying chance was two in ten thousand, the increase is one additional case in ten thousand. Both figures are correct; only the second tells you what to do. Headlines carry the first because it is larger, and readers who later encounter the absolute number reasonably feel misled.

There is also a quiet asymmetry in what gets published and reported. A trial finding no effect is less likely to be published and far less likely to be covered, so the visible evidence tilts toward positive findings that later fail to replicate. The correction, when it comes, looks like a reversal to the public and like normal operation to researchers.

The practical response is neither credulity nor dismissal. Ask what kind of study produced a claim, whether the risk is relative or absolute, and whether the recommendation is for a population or for you. Guidance that changes in response to better evidence is functioning as intended; guidance that never changes is the one worth worrying about.

passages.title: Should Employers Run Workplace Wellness Programmes?

viewpoints.name: Adaeze Nwachukwu, HR director
viewpoints.text: We run one and I will describe it accurately rather than well. Take-up is about a third, concentrated among staff who were already active, and I have never been able to show it reduced sick days — the studies claiming that are mostly employer-reported and I do not trust our own numbers either. What it did do is give people a reason to leave their desks at lunchtime, which the culture here previously discouraged. That is a smaller claim than the brochure makes and it is the one I can defend.

viewpoints.name: Dr Wren Halloway, occupational physician
viewpoints.text: My concern is what these programmes displace. A step-challenge is cheap, visible and popular with boards; fixing a shift pattern that guarantees short sleep is expensive, invisible and unpopular. The evidence that workload, control over your hours and job security drive health outcomes is far stronger than the evidence for any wellness app. I am not against the programmes. I am against them being counted as the health strategy when they are the easy part of it.

viewpoints.name: Ravi Sundaram, employee
viewpoints.text: The gym subsidy is genuinely useful and I use it. The health questionnaire is a different thing and I did not fill it in. I am told it is confidential and aggregated, and I believe the people telling me that, but the data still exists and I have no control over what happens to it in three years or under a different owner. Make the benefits available without requiring disclosure and my objection disappears entirely — it was never about the exercise.

viewpoints.name: Councillor Marta Lindqvist
viewpoints.text: I would ask who is left out. These programmes reach salaried staff with predictable hours and a lunch break. They do not reach shift workers, contractors or anyone on an hourly rate who loses money by attending. So the benefit lands on the healthiest, best-paid part of the workforce, and the health gap inside the same organisation gets wider rather than narrower. If an employer wants to improve health, start with the people the programme cannot currently reach.
